question: In a mass-casualty triage, a patient has respiratory rate 34/min, capillary refill time more than 2 seconds and follows simple commands. Which triage category is assigned?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Red – Priority I (immediate)

🧠 Clinical Rationale: In START triage a patient who is not ambulatory but has a respiratory rate above 30/min and delayed capillary refill is tagged Red (immediate), because life-saving intervention is needed within minutes

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Green – Priority III (minor): Green is only for walking wounded who can self-evacuate

B — Black – Priority IV (expectant): Black is for deceased or injuries beyond available resources, and this patient is conscious with a pulse

C — Yellow – Priority II (delayed): Yellow is for stable patients with delayed presentation, but here two red criteria are already present

⚠️ Exam Trap: Be careful with absolute words such as ALWAYS and NEVER unless the fact is truly absolute.

💎 PNC Pearl: Triage re-assessment is repeated at every transfer because category changes as the patient deteriorates

question: As per START triage, what is the FIRST step while sorting casualties at the scene of a bus accident?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Ask each victim to walk to a marked safe area

🧠 Clinical Rationale: START begins with a global sorting step: ambulatory casualties are moved aside as Priority III, which instantly reduces the crowd to be assessed

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Measure blood pressure of every victim: BP measurement is too slow and is not used to decide the initial walking category

B — Check pupillary reaction: Pupillary assessment belongs to neurological examination, not the first sorting step

C — Attach cardiac monitor to all victims: Monitoring is done after triage, in the treatment area

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: The first triage decision must take seconds, not minutes, so the tool is deliberately simple
option_4: Ask each victim to walk to a marked safe area

question: In disaster triage, the black tag indicates that the casualty:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Is deceased or has injuries beyond the resources available

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The black/expectant category covers casualties who are already dead or whose injuries exceed the resources available, so they are not treated while salvageable patients wait

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Is infectious and needs isolation: Infection control is a separate triage consideration and does not create a black tag

C — Requires surgery within one hour: Surgery within one hour is red

D — Has only minor injuries and may wait: Minor injuries are green

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Disaster triage prioritises doing the greatest good for the greatest number, so it differs from day-to-day emergency triage
option_1: Is deceased or has injuries beyond the resources available
option_4: Has only minor injuries and may wait

question: Shock is BEST defined as:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Inadequate tissue perfusion causing cellular hypoxia

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion in which oxygen delivery fails to meet cellular demand, and hypotension is only one late sign

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — A fall in systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg: Hypotension is a late feature; shock can exist with a normal blood pressure in compensated stages

B — Loss of consciousness after head injury: Loss of consciousness is a neurological finding that may or may not accompany shock

C — Decreased urine output below 30 mL/hour: Oliguria is a consequence of renal hypoperfusion, not the definition

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Treat shock before the blood pressure falls — tachycardia, cool peripheries and narrow pulse pressure are earlier warning signs
option_1: A fall in systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg

question: A 30-year-old man with a tibial fracture has pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 106/88 mmHg, cool extremities and capillary refill of 3 seconds. Which finding most strongly suggests compensated shock?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Heart rate of 124/min with narrowed pulse pressure

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Tachycardia with a narrowed pulse pressure (106/88, pressure difference only 18 mmHg) is the classic compensated stage of hypovolemic shock, where vasoconstriction preserves the systolic value

🔍 Key Clues: 30-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Systolic pressure of 106 mmHg: A systolic value above 90 mmHg alone does not exclude shock and is not the marker here

C — Warm extremities: Extremities in hypovolemic shock are cool, not warm

D — Tibial fracture: The fracture is the cause, not the haemodynamic sign

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: A "normal" blood pressure with tachycardia in trauma is a red flag — look for the bleeding source immediately
option_1: Heart rate of 124/min with narrowed pulse pressure

question: A patient develops urticaria, wheeze, stridor and hypotension within minutes of an intravenous antibiotic. Which is the FIRST drug to be given?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Adrenaline 0.5 mg intramuscularly

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Adrenaline is first-line in anaphylaxis: it reverses bronchospasm, supports the blood pressure and inhibits further mediator release, and intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh acts within minutes

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Chlorpheniramine 10 mg intravenously: Antihistamines relieve skin symptoms but do not reverse airway obstruction or hypotension

C — Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously: Steroids are given after adrenaline and act only over hours

D — Salbutamol nebulisation alone: A beta-2 agonist helps wheeze only and does not treat the cardiovascular collapse

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Stop the trigger, give adrenaline, call for help and lay the patient flat with legs raised

question: A 62-year-old man after an anterior wall myocardial infarction has blood pressure 84/60 mmHg, raised jugular venous pressure, bilateral basal crackles and cold peripheries. Which type of shock is present?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Cardiogenic

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Raised JVP with pulmonary crackles shows a failing pump with a fluid-loaded venous and pulmonary circuit, which is cardiogenic shock after a large infarct

🔍 Key Clues: 62-year-old

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Neurogenic: Neurogenic shock produces hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin

B — Hypovolemic: In hypovolemic shock the neck veins are flat because the vascular volume is depleted

C — Anaphylactic: Anaphylaxis is accompanied by urticaria, wheeze or angio-oedema and a warm vasodilated state

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: In cardiogenic shock, cautious fluid and early inotropic support are needed; a rapid fluid bolus can worsen pulmonary oedema

question: A patient with a cervical spine injury has blood pressure 76/46 mmHg, pulse 48/min and warm dry skin. Which shock type has the HIGHEST likelihood here?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Neurogenic

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Loss of sympathetic tone after spinal cord injury causes vasodilatation and unopposed vagal activity, giving the combination of hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Obstructive: Obstructive shock such as tension pneumothorax gives distended neck veins and unilateral absent breath sounds

B — Septic: Septic shock is usually accompanied by fever, tachycardia and vasodilatation with warm skin, but the pulse is fast and not slow

D — Haemorrhagic: Haemorrhagic shock shows cool clammy skin and tachycardia

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Neurogenic hypotension needs cautious volume and vasopressor support, and the spine must stay immobilised throughout

question: A 38-year-old woman is bleeding from a scalp laceration. At what stage of blood loss does a fall in systolic blood pressure usually become evident in a healthy adult?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. After about 30% loss

🧠 Clinical Rationale: In a previously healthy adult, hypotension appears after roughly 30% (about 1500 mL) loss, by which time tachycardia and narrowing of pulse pressure are well established

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — After about 10% loss: At 10% loss vital signs are practically normal

C — After about 15% loss: At 15% the pulse rises and anxiety appears, but the blood pressure is maintained

D — After about 45% loss: At 45% the patient is usually in decompensated shock with marked hypotension and altered consciousness

⚠️ Exam Trap: Be careful with absolute words such as ALWAYS and NEVER unless the fact is truly absolute.

💎 PNC Pearl: Never wait for hypotension to start fluid resuscitation and haemorrhage control

question: What is the recommended chest compression rate during adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 100–120 per minute

🧠 Clinical Rationale: High-quality CPR requires 100 to 120 compressions per minute; faster rates reduce compression depth and coronary perfusion

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 80–100 per minute: 80–100 per minute was an older recommendation and is no longer adequate

B — 60–80 per minute: Below 100 per minute delivers too few compressions and lowers the return of spontaneous circulation

C — 140–160 per minute: Above 120 per minute shortens diastolic filling and reduces depth

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Count aloud or use a metronome, and rotate the compressor every two minutes to prevent fatigue

question: What is the recommended compression depth for an average adult during CPR?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. 5–6 cm

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Adult compressions must depress the sternum 5 to 6 cm and allow complete chest recoil, which generates the thoracic pump pressure needed for cerebral and coronary flow

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — At least 4 cm: At least 4 cm sounds adequate but falls short of the recommended depth

B — 2–3 cm: 2–3 cm is the paediatric/infant scale and is far too shallow

D — 8–10 cm: 8–10 cm is excessive and increases rib and visceral injury

⚠️ Exam Trap: Be careful with absolute words such as ALWAYS and NEVER unless the fact is truly absolute.

💎 PNC Pearl: Allow full recoil between compressions, because venous return happens during the relaxation phase

question: In a single-rescuer adult CPR, what is the compression-to-ventilation ratio without an advanced airway?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 30:2

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The 30:2 ratio gives the minimum interruption to compressions while still providing some ventilation, and it is the standard for both single- and two-rescuer adult CPR before an advanced airway is placed

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 15:2: 15:2 applies to two-rescuer paediatric CPR

B — 5:1: 5:1 was replaced long ago because it caused excessive compression pauses

C — 50:5: There is no 50:5 ratio in any current guideline

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Once an advanced airway is secured, compressions become continuous at 100–120 per minute with one breath every 6 seconds

question: A monitored patient suddenly shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the CORRECT immediate sequence?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Defibrillate immediately, then resume CPR at once

🧠 Clinical Rationale: VF is a shockable rhythm, and the single most effective intervention is unsynchronised defibrillation as early as possible, followed immediately by compressions without a pulse check

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Give atropine and observe the rhythm: Atropine is used in symptomatic bradycardia and has no role in VF

C — Start chest compressions for five minutes before defibrillation: Delaying defibrillation lowers survival by roughly 7–10% for every minute lost

D — Give adrenaline, then defibrillate: Adrenaline is given after the second or third shock, not before defibrillation

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: The shock stops the chaotic electrical activity; CPR then delivers oxygen until an organised rhythm returns
option_2: Defibrillate immediately, then resume CPR at once
option_3: Start chest compressions for five minutes before defibrillation

question: As per the Rule of Nines in an adult, what percentage of total body surface area is contributed by one entire upper limb?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 9%

🧠 Clinical Rationale: In the adult Rule of Nines each upper limb is 9%, the head 9%, each lower limb 18%, the front trunk 18%, the back trunk 18% and the perineum 1%

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 18%: 18% is one whole lower limb or one whole trunk surface

B — 13.5%: 13.5% is not a standard segment in the adult chart

C — 4.5%: 4.5% is one half of a limb, or the anterior surface only

⚠️ Exam Trap: In FIRST-action questions, identify the life-threatening problem and stabilise or assess before anything else.

💎 PNC Pearl: The patient's palm including fingers is about 1% TBSA and is useful for small or patchy burns

question: A 60 kg man has 40% TBSA burns. Using the Parkland formula (4 mL × body weight in kg × %TBSA), how much Ringer lactate is required in the first 24 hours?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. 9600 mL

🧠 Clinical Rationale: 4 × 60 × 40 = 9600 mL over 24 hours, of which half (4800 mL) is given in the first 8 hours counted from the time of injury, not from the time of admission

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — 7200 mL: 7200 mL comes from using 3 mL instead of 4 mL per kg per percent

C — 4800 mL: 4800 mL is only the first 8-hour half

D — 14400 mL: 14400 mL over-resuscitates and risks pulmonary oedema

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults is the bedside guide for titrating the infusion

question: A worker spills a strong acid on his forearm. What is the FIRST measure at the scene?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Flush the area with copious running water for at least 20 minutes

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Immediate copious water irrigation dilutes and removes the chemical, limits the depth of injury and is the single most effective first aid step

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Apply antibiotic ointment and bandage: Ointment traps residual chemical against the skin

C — Pop the blisters to release the acid: Blister deroofing invites infection; blisters are left intact in the emergency phase

D — Neutralise with an alkaline solution: Chemical neutralisation generates heat and causes an additional thermal burn

⚠️ Exam Trap: Do not pick an option only because it is familiar - the option that fits the whole stem is the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Irrigation for chemical burns is started before anything else, and contaminated clothing is removed while flushing
option_2: Flush the area with copious running water for at least 20 minutes
option_3: Pop the blisters to release the acid

question: On the third day after a full-thickness circumferential burn of the chest, the patient becomes restless with rising peak airway pressure. Which complication should the nurse suspect FIRST?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Restriction of chest expansion by the inelastic eschar

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A circumferential full-thickness eschar is inelastic; as oedema increases it restricts chest wall excursion, so ventilation pressure rises and the patient becomes hypoxic and restless — an escharotomy may be needed

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Anxiety reaction: Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion once hypoxia has been ruled out

B — Hyponatraemia: Sodium imbalance develops more slowly and does not raise airway pressure

C — Gastric dilatation: Gastric dilatation can splint the diaphragm but does not produce the same rising pressure pattern alone

⚠️ Exam Trap: Read the stem twice - one word such as MOST or EXCEPT can reverse the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Full-thickness burns are painless and leathery; it is the tight eschar over chest or limb, not the burn depth, that threatens ventilation and perfusion
option_4: Restriction of chest expansion by the inelastic eschar

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate for a healthy adult?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 12–20 per minute

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The accepted adult range is 12 to 20 breaths per minute, assessed with the chest exposed while the patient is unaware of being counted

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 24–30 per minute: Above 20 per minute in an adult is tachypnoea and signals respiratory distress or metabolic acidosis

B — 30–40 per minute: 30–40 per minute is the normal range for a newborn

C — 8–10 per minute: Below 12 per minute is bradypnoea

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Respiratory rate is the most sensitive early vital sign and also the one most often recorded by estimation rather than by counting a full minute

question: The normal adult resting pulse rate is:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. 60–100 per minute

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A resting adult pulse of 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal, though trained athletes may sit comfortably at 50

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — 120–140 per minute: This rate in a resting adult is a significant tachycardia requiring assessment

C — 100–120 per minute: Above 100 per minute is tachycardia, which is an early compensatory response to fever, pain, hypoxia or blood loss

D — 40–60 per minute: Below 60 per minute is bradycardia and may be physiological in athletes or pathological in heart block

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Always record rate along with rhythm, volume and character, because a bounding or thready pulse changes the interpretation

question: Which blood pressure reading is classified as normal for a healthy adult?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 100/70 mmHg

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A systolic below 120 mmHg with a diastolic below 80 mmHg is the normal adult classification

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 135/88 mmHg: 135/88 falls in the prehypertensive/high-normal band and needs lifestyle advice and follow-up

B — 165/100 mmHg: 165/100 is stage 2 hypertension and needs prompt medical review

C — 145/95 mmHg: 145/95 is stage 1 hypertension

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: A single high reading does not diagnose hypertension; confirm with repeated measurements on separate occasions

question: Which single measure is most effective in preventing health-care-associated infection?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Hand hygiene at the correct moments

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact remains the most effective, cheapest way to break the chain of transmission

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Isolating every patient with a fever: Isolation is reserved for confirmed or suspected transmissible infection and cannot be applied to every febrile patient

B — Prophylactic antibiotics: Routine prophylaxis breeds resistance and does not prevent organism transfer

D — Wearing gloves for all patient contact: Gloves protect the wearer but become contaminated like hands and never replace hand hygiene

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Contaminated hands are the commonest vehicle of cross-infection, so hand hygiene is audited as a key patient-safety indicator

question: As per WHO, the "five moments for hand hygiene" do NOT include washing hands:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Before completing documentation at the nursing station

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The five moments cover before patient contact, before an aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after patient contact and after touching patient surroundings; writing notes away from the bedside is not one of them

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Before touching a patient: Before touching a patient is Moment 1

C — After body fluid exposure risk: After body fluid exposure risk is Moment 3

D — After touching patient surroundings: After touching patient surroundings is Moment 5

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: The five moments are defined around the patient zone, which is why the sequence is decided by what you are about to touch, not by how dirty it looks
option_1: Before completing documentation at the nursing station

question: How often should the cardiac arrest trolley (crash cart) and defibrillator be checked?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Every shift, with the checklist signed

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The trolley and defibrillator are checked at the start of every shift and after every use, and the checklist is signed so that accountability is documented

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Once a month: Monthly checking leaves expired drugs and a discharged defibrillator battery in service for weeks

B — Only after a code blue is used: Checking only after use assumes the equipment is otherwise intact

C — Once a week only: A weekly check still allows a whole week of undetected deficiency

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Checks include seal, expiry dates, battery charge, laryngoscope light and suction function — an unsealed cart loses its guarantee
option_2: Only after a code blue is used

question: Which position is BEST for an unconscious patient who is breathing and has no suspected spinal injury, while awaiting review?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Left lateral recovery position

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The lateral recovery position keeps the tongue forward and lets secretions or vomit drain out, protecting the airway while maintaining spontaneous breathing

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Supine with a pillow under the head: Supine position allows the tongue to fall back and increases aspiration risk

C — Sitting upright with legs dependent: An upright position is unsafe in an unconscious patient and may worsen cerebral perfusion

D — Prone with the head turned to one side: Prone positioning is used in ventilated ARDS patients under supervision, not as a routine recovery position

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Any spinal suspicion overrides this choice; the airway is then maintained with manual in-line immobilisation
option_2: Supine with a pillow under the head
option_4: Prone with the head turned to one side

question: While setting up a sterile field, which part of the sterile drape is considered contaminated?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. The outer border of about one inch (2.5 cm)

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The outer one-inch border of a sterile package or drape is considered unsterile because it may have been touched or exposed during storage, so instruments are kept away from the edge

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — The part under the instrument tray: Instruments rest on the sterile area, which does not contaminate the drape

B — The whole drape once the pack is opened: The drape is sterile as long as it is not wet, not below waist level and not out of sight

D — The centre of the drape: The centre remains sterile if kept above waist level and kept in view

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: Sterile objects must remain within the field of vision and above waist level; if you cannot see it, you must consider it contaminated
option_2: The whole drape once the pack is opened
option_3: The outer border of about one inch (2.5 cm)

question: Which action is acceptable while maintaining a patient's clinical record?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Correcting an error with a single line, the corrected entry, date, time and signature

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The accepted legal method is to strike a single line through the error, write the correct entry and append date, time and signature, so the original remains readable

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Leaving the entry unsigned to save time: An unsigned entry has no legal standing

C — Erasing the wrong entry so the record looks neat: Erasing or using correction fluid destroys the legal value of the record and may be treated as tampering

D — Writing the entry a day later from memory: Late entries written from memory are unreliable and are usually identified as such

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: The record is a legal document, so it must be factual, timely, in sequence and free of abbreviations that others cannot interpret
option_1: Correcting an error with a single line, the corrected entry, date, time and signature
option_2: Leaving the entry unsigned to save time
option_3: Erasing the wrong entry so the record looks neat
option_4: Writing the entry a day later from memory

question: Which is the FIRST step of the nursing process?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Assessment

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Assessment gathers subjective and objective data and forms the base on which every later step depends

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Planning: Planning comes after the data are collected and the problem is identified

C — Implementation: Implementation follows planning and can only be correct if the assessment was correct

D — Evaluation: Evaluation is the final step, comparing the outcome with the goal

⚠️ Exam Trap: In procedure questions choose the step that protects the patient first - safety before comfort and speed.

💎 PNC Pearl: The nursing process is cyclical; evaluation findings feed back into a fresh assessment, which is why it is never a one-time exercise

question: A patient is found unresponsive with no breathing and no pulse. Which is the correct drug sequence during adult cardiac arrest?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Adrenaline 1 mg after the first cycle of CPR, repeated every 3–5 minutes

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Adrenaline 1 mg intravenous/intraosseous is given as soon as a rhythm check permits (in shockable rhythms it follows the shock cycle) and repeated every 3 to 5 minutes, in the standard 1 mg dose and not by escalating dose

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Sodium bicarbonate after the first rhythm check: Bicarbonate is not routine; it is reserved for specific circumstances such as documented hyperkalaemia or tricyclic overdose

C — Adrenaline 3 mg bolus once only: A 3 mg single bolus is not the recommended regimen and does not replace repeated dosing

D — Atropine first, then adrenaline: Atropine is not indicated in cardiac arrest and was removed from the algorithm years ago

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Adrenaline improves coronary perfusion pressure, so high-quality compressions continue while it is being drawn up
option_1: Sodium bicarbonate after the first rhythm check
option_2: Adrenaline 1 mg after the first cycle of CPR, repeated every 3–5 minutes

question: Which drug is the FIRST-line choice for symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Atropine

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Atropine 0.5 mg intravenously, repeated up to a maximum of 3 mg, blocks vagal tone and restores the rate in symptomatic bradycardia

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Amiodarone: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation

B — Digoxin: Digoxin slows conduction and would worsen the bradycardia

D — Adenosine: Adenosine is given for supraventricular tachycardia and produces transient asystole, which is hazardous here

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: If atropine fails, prepare for transcutaneous pacing or an adrenaline infusion while expert help is called

question: For a patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD, what oxygen saturation target should the nurse maintain?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. 88–92%

🧠 Clinical Rationale: In COPD with chronic carbon dioxide retention, controlled oxygen aiming at 88 to 92% avoids losing the hypoxic drive while correcting dangerous hypoxaemia

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 100%: 100% oxygen risks carbon dioxide narcosis in a CO2 retainer

B — 94–98%: 94–98% is the target for most other acutely ill adults

D — 70–80%: Below 88% leaves the patient hypoxic and at risk of arrhythmia and organ damage

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Use a controlled device such as a Venturi mask and re-check arterial blood gases after 30 to 60 minutes of therapy

question: A trauma patient in hypovolaemic shock needs urgent volume replacement. Which fluid is the first-line choice while blood is arranged?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Ringer lactate or 0.9% normal saline

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Warm isotonic crystalloid such as Ringer lactate or 0.9% saline restores intravascular volume and does not cause haemolysis or hypoglycaemia

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 5% dextrose: 5% dextrose distributes into total body water and leaves the vascular space within minutes, so it does not restore perfusion

C — 25% mannitol: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used for raised intracranial pressure, and it worsens hypovolaemia

D — 10% dextrose with potassium: Hypertonic dextrose with potassium is hazardous in shock and renal impairment

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Crystalloid is a bridge, not a substitute for blood; in ongoing haemorrhage, give blood products early and reassess continually

question: A patient brought to the casualty is drowsy with pin-point pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 per minute after suspected opioid overdose. Which drug should the nurse keep ready?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Naloxone

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that reverses the respiratory depression within minutes, and the dose is titrated to restore adequate breathing rather than full alertness

🔍 Key Clues: 6 per minute

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Flumazenil: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which cause central depression without pin-point pupils

C — N-acetylcysteine: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning

D — Physostigmine: Physostigmine is used in specific anticholinergic toxicity and is not an opioid antidote

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Naloxone acts briefly, so the patient must be monitored for re-sedation and the infusion repeated if needed

question: Morphine is prescribed for a patient with a fracture and severe pain. Which assessment is MOST important after administration?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Respiratory rate and depth

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Opioids depress the medullary respiratory centre, so the rate and depth of breathing must be monitored closely, along with the level of consciousness

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Pupillary size: Pin-point pupils are expected with opioids and are not the priority problem

B — Presence of ankle oedema: Peripheral oedema is not an acute opioid effect

D — Colour of the urine: Urine colour is unrelated to opioid effect

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Keep naloxone and oxygen available; also monitor for nausea, constipation and urinary retention, which are common opioid effects in the ward

question: A patient in anaphylaxis with hypotension has an adrenaline infusion prescribed at 0.05 microgram/kg/minute for a 60 kg adult. How many micrograms per minute is delivered?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 3 micrograms/min

🧠 Clinical Rationale: 0.05 × 60 = 3 micrograms per minute; the infusion is then titrated against the blood pressure and heart rate

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 0.3 microgram/min: 0.3 microgram/min equals 0.005 microgram/kg/min, which is ten times too low

B — 30 micrograms/min: 30 micrograms/min equals 0.5 microgram/kg/min, ten times too high

C — 300 micrograms/min: 300 micrograms/min would cause severe tachycardia and arrhythmia

⚠️ Exam Trap: Check the dose, route and timing before choosing - the right drug in the wrong dose is a wrong answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Vasopressor infusions are always delivered through a pump with the line checked for patency, because tissue extravasation of adrenaline can cause local necrosis

question: Which stage of labour extends from full cervical dilatation to the birth of the baby?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Second stage

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The second stage begins at full dilatation (10 cm) and ends with expulsion of the fetus; in a primigravida it usually lasts up to two hours

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Third stage: The third stage is from birth of the baby to expulsion of the placenta

C — Fourth stage: The fourth stage is the first hour or two after delivery, when the mother is observed for bleeding

D — First stage: The first stage runs from the onset of true labour to full dilatation

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: During the second stage the mother is encouraged to bear down with contractions while the fetal heart rate is checked every five minutes or after every contraction

question: Which is the FIRST action when a woman has heavy vaginal bleeding 20 minutes after a normal vaginal delivery?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Rub up the uterus and give the prescribed uterotonic while calling for help

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of post-partum haemorrhage, so uterine massage plus an oxytocic drug while summoning help controls most cases quickly

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Call the doctor and wait: Waiting wastes the critical first minutes, when the bleeding is easiest to control

C — Start a blood transfusion: Cross-matched blood is arranged after immediate measures and fluids are started, not before

D — Shift the patient to the labour ward: The woman stays where she is; help and equipment come to her

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: Post-partum haemorrhage is defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more after vaginal birth, or any loss causing haemodynamic instability
option_1: Rub up the uterus and give the prescribed uterotonic while calling for help
option_4: Shift the patient to the labour ward

question: Under the current Indian antenatal care schedule, how many minimum antenatal visits are recommended for a normal pregnancy?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. 4 visits

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Under the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan and the National Health Mission, a minimum of four antenatal visits is the accepted standard, with the first visit ideally in the first trimester

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 3 visits: Three visits miss the critical early registration

C — 2 visits: Two visits cannot screen for anaemia, hypertension or fetal growth in the third trimester

D — 8 visits: Eight visits follows the WHO 2016 model, which is desirable, but the minimum assured schedule in India remains four

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: Each visit has a defined purpose — early registration, screening, growth assessment and birth preparedness

question: The partograph plots cervical dilatation against time. Which pattern indicates the need for referral?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Dilatation crossing to the right of the alert line

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Progress slower than 1 cm per hour, shown as the plot entering the area to the right of the alert line, warns of prolonged labour and possible cephalopelvic disproportion

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Contractions every 3 minutes lasting 45 seconds: This is an adequate contraction pattern in the active phase

B — Dilatation of 1 cm per hour: 1 cm per hour in the active phase is the expected rate

C — Dilatation to the left of the alert line: Plotting to the left means labour is progressing faster than average and is not a warning

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: The action line lies four hours to the right of the alert line; crossing it means the woman needs immediate obstetric review and possible referral
option_3: Dilatation to the left of the alert line
option_4: Dilatation crossing to the right of the alert line

question: When should breastfeeding ideally be initiated after a normal vaginal delivery?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Within the first hour of birth

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Early initiation within the first hour, with skin-to-skin contact, improves breastfeeding success and provides colostrum rich in immunoglobulins

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Only when the mother feels milk let-down: Milk let-down occurs with suckling, so waiting for it delays both colostrum intake and the establishment of supply

C — After 6 hours once the mother rests: Delaying six hours reduces suckling success and delays milk production

D — After the first bath of the newborn: Bathing is deliberately postponed; it is not a reason to delay feeding

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: Colostrum within the first hour also stimulates uterine contractions and reduces post-partum haemorrhage risk
option_1: Only when the mother feels milk let-down
option_4: After the first bath of the newborn

question: Which contraceptive method is MOST suitable for a woman who has completed her family and wants a permanent method?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Tubectomy (female sterilisation)

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Bilateral tubal ligation is a permanent method intended for women who do not want further children, and it is performed under the national family planning programme

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Combined oral contraceptive pills: Oral pills are a temporary, reversible method needing daily compliance

B — Copper-T 380A insertion: Copper-T is a long-acting reversible method and can be removed if desired

D — Male condom use: Condoms are a temporary barrier method, also offering protection against sexually transmitted infections

⚠️ Exam Trap: In obstetric questions ask who is at immediate risk, mother or fetus - that decides the first action.

💎 PNC Pearl: Counselling must explain that sterilisation is essentially irreversible and must be voluntary, with written informed consent

question: Under the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme, what is the treatment given to a newly diagnosed TB patient in the intensive phase?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Four drugs for two months

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The intensive phase uses four first-line drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) for two months, followed by the continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampicin

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Two drugs for two months: Two drugs alone in the intensive phase risks the emergence of resistance

B — One drug daily for one year: Monotherapy is never used in tuberculosis and would create resistance rapidly

D — Three drugs for six months: Three drugs for six months omits ethambutol and shortens the intensive phase

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: Doses are given by weight band, and the continuation phase continues for four months, making six months the total duration for a new case

question: As per the Universal Immunisation Programme, at what age is the first dose of measles-rubella vaccine given in India?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. At 9–12 months

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The first measles-rubella dose is given at 9 to 12 months, when maternal antibodies have declined enough for the vaccine to take effect, and a second dose follows at 16 to 24 months

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — At 6 weeks: At 6 weeks the schedule covers pentavalent, oral polio and rotavirus

B — At 5 years: A booster of diphtheria-tetanus is given at 5 years; measles-rubella is not first given then

D — At birth: At birth only BCG, Hepatitis B birth dose and oral polio zero dose are given

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: Vitamin A is given with the measles-rubella dose at this visit, so it must be recorded on the same card

question: Which level of health care does a Community Health Centre represent?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Secondary

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Community Health Centres are first-referral units with specialists, so they belong to the secondary level of care

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Primary: The primary level comprises sub-centres, primary health centres and health and wellness centres

C — Quaternary: Quaternary is not part of the national three-tier structure

D — Tertiary: Tertiary care means district hospitals and above, with super-specialty services

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: Referral flows upwards from primary to secondary to tertiary, and the nurse's role includes preparing the patient and family for each transition

question: What is the recommended temperature range for storing vaccines in a vaccine carrier or ILR cold box at the field level?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. +2°C to +8°C

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Almost all routine vaccines must be kept between 2°C and 8°C, and vaccine vial monitors show whether the heat exposure has crossed the limit

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — +10°C to +15°C: A range of +10°C to +15°C is above the recommended range and allows progressive loss of potency

C — +20°C to +25°C: A range of +20°C to +25°C is far too warm and destroys vaccine potency quickly

D — −20°C to −10°C: Deep-freeze temperatures freeze and destroy the adsorbed vaccines such as DPT and hepatitis B

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: Freezing is the commonest cold-chain error; place ice packs conditioned so they do not touch the vials directly, and never store vaccines in the door of the refrigerator

question: Which measure is used for the control of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the vector of dengue?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Eliminating stagnant water in containers around homes

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Aedes aegypti breeds in clean stagnant water collected in pots, tyres and tanks, so source reduction — emptying and covering such containers — is the mainstay of dengue control

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Indoor residual spraying with DDT: Indoor residual spraying targets the resting malaria vector and is not the primary dengue measure

C — Mass administration of an antimalarial: Antimalarials have no effect on a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito

D — Insecticide-treated bed nets: Bed nets protect mostly against night-biting mosquitoes such as Anopheles, whereas Aedes bites during the day

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: The Aedes mosquito bites in the early morning and late afternoon, so day-time personal protection is important until fever settles
option_1: Eliminating stagnant water in containers around homes

question: The Infant Mortality Rate is expressed as the number of deaths of infants under one year per:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. 1,000 live births

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Infant mortality rate equals infant deaths under one year in a year divided by live births in the same year, multiplied by 1,000

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 1,000 mid-year population: Population is the denominator for crude death rate, not for IMR

C — 100 live births: Using 100 as the denominator gives a five-fold exaggeration

D — 1,00,000 population: 1,00,000 is the denominator used for maternal mortality ratio in some presentations, not for IMR

⚠️ Exam Trap: In community health questions ask whether the action is at family, community or facility level.

💎 PNC Pearl: The numerator includes all deaths from birth up to but not including the first birthday, and both neonatal and post-neonatal deaths are counted

question: What is the correct way to prepare Oral Rehydration Solution from the standard packet?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Mix one packet in one litre of clean water and use within 24 hours

🧠 Clinical Rationale: One packet dissolved in exactly one litre of clean, preferably boiled and cooled water gives the correct osmolarity, and the prepared solution is discarded after 24 hours

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Mix one packet in one litre of milk: Milk changes the composition and breeds bacteria quickly

C — Add extra sugar to make it more palatable: Extra sugar makes the solution hyperosmolar and increases stool output

D — Mix one packet in half a litre of boiling water: Half a litre makes a hypertonic solution that can worsen diarrhoea

⚠️ Exam Trap: In paediatric questions look at the age first - the normal values and the expected action change with age.

💎 PNC Pearl: Continue breastfeeding alongside ORS and add zinc for 14 days in children with diarrhoea, as per the national programme
option_1: Mix one packet in one litre of milk
option_2: Mix one packet in one litre of clean water and use within 24 hours
option_3: Add extra sugar to make it more palatable
option_4: Mix one packet in half a litre of boiling water

question: Kangaroo Mother Care involves:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby with exclusive breastfeeding

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Kangaroo Mother Care is continuous skin-to-skin contact on the mother's chest, with frequent exclusive breastfeeding and close follow-up; it maintains temperature, aids weight gain and reduces mortality in low-birth-weight babies

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Keeping the baby in an incubator with humidified oxygen: The incubator provides warmth but not the contact and feeding benefits of KMC

B — Wrapping the baby in multiple woollen layers only: Wrapping alone gives warmth without the physiological and feeding advantages

C — Feeding the baby by nasogastric tube every two hours: Tube feeding is used when suckling is not possible, but it is not KMC

⚠️ Exam Trap: In paediatric questions look at the age first - the normal values and the expected action change with age.

💎 PNC Pearl: In KMC the baby should be kept upright between the breasts, with the head turned to the side so the airway stays clear
option_1: Keeping the baby in an incubator with humidified oxygen
option_2: Wrapping the baby in multiple woollen layers only
option_3: Feeding the baby by nasogastric tube every two hours
option_4: Skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby with exclusive breastfeeding

question: A social smile in an infant is normally present by the age of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. 2 months

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A responsive social smile appears at about 2 months and is an early marker of intact vision and social development

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 9 months: By 9 months the infant sits without support, may stand holding on and shows stranger anxiety

B — 2 weeks: At 2 weeks the smile is usually a reflex during sleep or wind

D — 6 months: By 6 months the infant laughs, reaches for objects and turns towards sound

⚠️ Exam Trap: In paediatric questions look at the age first - the normal values and the expected action change with age.

💎 PNC Pearl: Regression or absence of expected milestones calls for developmental screening and referral

question: What is the most important nursing measure during phototherapy for neonatal jaundice?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Covering the eyes and genitals and ensuring adequate fluid intake

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The eyes are shielded from retinal damage, the gonads are covered, and hydration plus frequent feeds help excrete the bilirubin through urine and stool

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Applying oil to the skin before the session: Oils and lotions can burn the skin and must be avoided

C — Keeping the baby fully covered between light cycles: The baby is kept undressed except for the covers, so maximum skin surface is exposed to light

D — Stopping breastfeeding during therapy: Breastfeeding is continued because frequent feeding increases bilirubin clearance

⚠️ Exam Trap: In paediatric questions look at the age first - the normal values and the expected action change with age.

💎 PNC Pearl: Monitor temperature, weight and bilirubin levels, and watch for bronze baby syndrome and dehydration during therapy
option_1: Covering the eyes and genitals and ensuring adequate fluid intake
option_2: Applying oil to the skin before the session
option_3: Keeping the baby fully covered between light cycles

question: Complementary feeds should be started for an infant at the age of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. 6 completed months

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months and then complementary feeding with continued breastfeeding up to two years is the national recommendation, because before six months the gut and kidneys are not ready for other foods

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — 12 months: By 12 months the child should already be on family food with breastfeeding continued, so starting then is far too late

C — 2 months: At 2 months exclusive breastfeeding is essential

D — 4 months: At 4 months breast milk alone still meets all needs

⚠️ Exam Trap: In paediatric questions look at the age first - the normal values and the expected action change with age.

💎 PNC Pearl: The first complementary food is usually a mashed cereal or dal with no added salt or sugar, and one new food is introduced at a time

question: Which valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Mitral valve

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left atrioventricular opening and prevents backflow into the left atrium during ventricular systole

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Tricuspid valve: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle

B — Aortic valve: The aortic valve is at the outlet of the left ventricle

C — Pulmonary valve: The pulmonary valve is at the outlet of the right ventricle

⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the definition AND the unit - exams love near-sounding concepts.

💎 PNC Pearl: Mitral stenosis obstructs filling of the left ventricle and causes pulmonary congestion, which is why the earliest symptoms are breathlessness

question: Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs takes place at the level of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Alveoli

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Alveoli have a thin single-cell wall and a rich capillary network, so gas diffusion occurs across the alveolar-capillary membrane

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Bronchi: Bronchi are conducting airways with cartilage and no gas exchange surface

B — Trachea: The trachea is a pure conduit

C — Pleura: The pleura is a serous membrane that reduces friction, not a diffusing surface

⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the definition AND the unit - exams love near-sounding concepts.

💎 PNC Pearl: In pulmonary oedema, fluid collects in the alveoli and widens the diffusion distance, so the patient becomes hypoxic even with a normal respiratory rate

question: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Nephron

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The nephron, comprising the glomerulus, tubules and collecting duct, performs filtration, reabsorption and secretion

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Loop of Henle alone: The loop of Henle is one segment that concentrates urine but is not the whole unit

B — Renal pelvis: The renal pelvis is a collecting funnel that drains into the ureter

D — Glomerulus alone: The glomerulus is only the filter element of the nephron

⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the definition AND the unit - exams love near-sounding concepts.

💎 PNC Pearl: About one million nephrons exist in each kidney, and damage to more than half of them is needed before the serum creatinine rises noticeably, so early renal injury is easily missed

question: Which of the following is a long bone of the human body?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Femur

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The femur has a shaft with two expanded ends, making it a typical long bone, and it is the longest bone in the body

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Vertebra: A vertebra is an irregular bone with a complex shape

C — Sternum: The sternum is a flat bone that protects the mediastinum

D — Scapula: The scapula is a flat bone of the shoulder girdle

⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the definition AND the unit - exams love near-sounding concepts.

💎 PNC Pearl: Long bones contain red marrow in the metaphysis, which is why the femur and humerus are common sites of bone marrow aspiration in children

question: Which component of the Mental Status Examination assesses the patient's awareness of time, place and person?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Orientation

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Orientation is tested by asking the date, the place and the identity of the people around, and its loss follows the pattern of time first, then place, then person

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Thought content: Thought content covers delusions, obsessions and suicidal ideas

C — Insight: Insight is the patient's awareness of his own illness

D — Judgement: Judgement is tested with a hypothetical problem-solving question

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Disorientation is commoner in delirium than in functional illness, so its presence should prompt a search for a physical cause

question: A patient says, "Everyone would be better off if I were gone." What is the nurse's MOST appropriate response?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. "Are you thinking about ending your life?"

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A direct, calm question about suicidal thoughts assesses the risk, conveys that the nurse is willing to hear it and does not plant the idea

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — "Let us talk about something more pleasant.": Changing the subject tells the patient that the nurse is not available

B — "You should not talk like that.": A statement of that kind closes the conversation and increases isolation

D — "You have a lot to live for.": Reassurance dismisses the patient's feelings and cuts off exploration

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Any expression of hopelessness in a patient with depression calls for direct risk assessment, close observation and removal of potentially dangerous items
option_1: "Let us talk about something more pleasant."
option_3: "Are you thinking about ending your life?"
option_4: "You have a lot to live for."

question: A student who is angry with his teacher joins the college athletics team and channels his energy into training. This is an example of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Sublimation

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Sublimation is the mature defence in which an unacceptable impulse is redirected into a socially acceptable and productive activity

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Denial: Denial refuses to accept the reality of a distressing fact

C — Projection: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to another person

D — Regression: Regression is a return to behaviour of an earlier developmental stage

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Sublimation and humour are considered mature defences because they preserve functioning and relationships

question: What are the standard parameters for steam sterilization in an autoclave?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. 121°C at 15 psi for 15–20 minutes

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Moist heat at 121°C and 15 pounds per square inch for 15 to 20 minutes kills spores by denaturing proteins in the presence of moisture

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 180°C at 20 psi for 5 minutes: 180°C with pressure is not a valid autoclave setting

C — 60°C at 5 psi for 30 minutes: 60°C is a pasteurisation range and does not sterilise

D — 100°C at 10 psi for 60 minutes: Boiling at 100°C kills most vegetative organisms but not spores

⚠️ Exam Trap: Separate sterilisation from disinfection, and bacteria from viruses - they are common distractors.

💎 PNC Pearl: Sterility must be verified with an indicator such as a Bowie-Dick tape and periodic biological spore testing, not by appearance of the pack

question: The complete destruction of all micro-organisms including spores from an article is termed:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Sterilization

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Sterilization removes or kills all microbial life, including bacterial spores, and is required for surgical instruments and implants

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Disinfection: Disinfection reduces but does not reliably eliminate spores on inanimate objects

B — Antisepsis: Antisepsis is chemical disinfection of living tissue such as skin

C — Sanitisation: Sanitisation lowers the number of organisms to a safe level, as in cleaning utensils

⚠️ Exam Trap: Separate sterilisation from disinfection, and bacteria from viruses - they are common distractors.

💎 PNC Pearl: Critical items that enter sterile tissue must be sterilised, while semi-critical items touching mucous membranes require high-level disinfection

question: Which of the following is NOT a cardinal sign of acute inflammation?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Pallor

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The five cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function; pallor is not one of them because vasodilatation increases local blood flow

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Pain: Pain results from chemical mediators and pressure on nerve endings

B — Heat: Heat is produced by increased blood flow at the inflamed site

C — Redness: Redness comes from vasodilatation and increased flow

⚠️ Exam Trap: Distinguish acute from chronic, and reversible from irreversible, before choosing.

💎 PNC Pearl: Whereas inflammation is a protective response, pallor with coldness usually indicates reduced perfusion and should be reported

question: Which phase of wound healing is characterised by the formation of granulation tissue and collagen deposition?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Proliferative phase

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The proliferative phase, roughly from day 4 to day 21, builds new capillaries and collagen to fill the defect

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Haemostasis: Haemostasis is the immediate clot formation phase

C — Inflammatory phase: The inflammatory phase is dominated by neutrophils and macrophages clearing debris

D — Remodelling phase: Remodelling strengthens and reorganises the collagen over months

⚠️ Exam Trap: Distinguish acute from chronic, and reversible from irreversible, before choosing.

💎 PNC Pearl: Protein, vitamin C and zinc are required for collagen synthesis, so malnutrition is a common cause of delayed healing

question: Bleeding gums, delayed wound healing and petechiae in a malnourished patient suggest a deficiency of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Vitamin C

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline in collagen, so its deficiency causes capillary fragility, bleeding gums and poor wound healing

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Vitamin K: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time and causes bleeding, but not bleeding gums with poor healing

C — Vitamin D: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults

D — Vitamin A: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia

⚠️ Exam Trap: Separate the deficiency disease from its dietary source - exams mix the two.

💎 PNC Pearl: Fresh fruits and vegetables are the main sources, and requirements rise during sepsis, burns and post-operative recovery

question: In which method of nursing care delivery does a group of nurses led by a team leader provide total care to a group of patients?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Team nursing

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Team nursing uses a team leader who delegates care according to the skills of members, which suits wards with a mixed skill mix

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Primary nursing: Primary nursing gives one nurse 24-hour responsibility for the care plan of assigned patients

B — Case method: The case method assigns one nurse to one patient for the entire shift

D — Functional nursing: Functional nursing divides work by task, so no one owns the patient's total care

⚠️ Exam Trap: Remember that delegation transfers the task but never the accountability.

💎 PNC Pearl: Whatever the model, responsibility for supervision and correct delegation cannot be delegated away

question: In the research process, the statement that predicts the relationship between two variables is called the:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Hypothesis

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A hypothesis is a testable prediction about the relationship between an independent and a dependent variable, and the study is designed to accept or reject it

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Sample: A sample is the subset of the population selected for study

B — Variable: A variable is any characteristic that can vary and be measured

D — Limitation: Limitations are the constraints in design or method acknowledged by the researcher

⚠️ Exam Trap: In research questions define the term precisely - reliability, validity and sampling are often interchanged.

💎 PNC Pearl: A null hypothesis states there is no relationship, and statistical testing decides whether it can be rejected

question: What is the normal serum sodium concentration in an adult?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. 135–145 mEq/L

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Normal serum sodium is 135 to 145 mEq/L and is the chief determinant of extracellular fluid osmolality

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 100–120 mEq/L: Below 120 mEq/L is severe hyponatraemia, which can cause seizures

B — 3.5–5.0 mEq/L: 3.5–5.0 mEq/L is the normal serum potassium range, not sodium

D — 150–170 mEq/L: 150–170 mEq/L is hypernatraemia

⚠️ Exam Trap: Beware near-sounding options and units - define the quantity before choosing.

💎 PNC Pearl: Sodium disorders are disorders of water balance, so treatment depends on the volume status rather than on the sodium value alone

question: Retaining a new telephone number by repeating it aloud several times is an example of:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Short-term (working) memory maintained by rehearsal

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Repeating information keeps it in short-term memory, which holds a limited amount of data for seconds unless it is rehearsed or encoded

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Long-term memory: Long-term memory requires encoding and consolidation, not mere repetition

B — Implicit memory: Implicit memory is procedural recall such as riding a cycle

C — Sensory memory: Sensory memory lasts under a second after the stimulus ends

⚠️ Exam Trap: In mental health questions, choose the response that is non-judgemental and preserves safety first.

💎 PNC Pearl: Giving written instructions and repeating key teaching points aids encoding, which matters greatly in patient education

question: A family consisting of parents and their unmarried children living together is called a:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. Nuclear family

🧠 Clinical Rationale: A nuclear family comprises two generations — parents and their dependent children — living in one household

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Extended family: An extended family adds other relatives such as grandparents and cousins

B — Joint family: A joint family has two or more related couples with their children under one roof or in one household unit

C — Single-parent family: A single-parent family has one parent with children

⚠️ Exam Trap: Look for the qualifier (FIRST / BEST / MOST LIKELY) - it decides the answer.

💎 PNC Pearl: Family structure decides who will provide care and finance treatment, so it must be assessed before discharge planning

question: A disorder appears in every generation and affects both males and females equally. Which pattern of inheritance does this suggest?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Autosomal dominant

🧠 Clinical Rationale: An autosomal dominant trait needs only one affected allele, so it appears in every generation with horizontal transmission and equal sex distribution

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Mitochondrial: Mitochondrial disorders are passed from mother to all children

C — X-linked recessive: X-linked recessive disorders show a marked excess of affected males and carrier females

D — Autosomal recessive: Autosomal recessive disorders typically appear in siblings with unaffected carrier parents

⚠️ Exam Trap: For genetic questions work out the pattern of inheritance before the probability.

💎 PNC Pearl: A dominant condition means each pregnancy carries a 50% risk, which is the basis of genetic counselling for the family

question: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of valid informed consent?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Signature of the hospital security officer

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Informed consent rests on information, comprehension, capacity and voluntariness; an administrative or security signature is not a legal element of consent

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Adequate information given to the patient: Reasonable information about the nature, risks and alternatives is essential

B — The patient's capacity to decide: The patient must be competent to understand and decide

D — Voluntariness without coercion: The decision must be free of pressure from staff or family

⚠️ Exam Trap: In legal and ethical questions ask WHO has the authority to act, not who is present.

💎 PNC Pearl: In an emergency where the patient cannot consent and no relative is available, treatment proceeds under the doctrine of implied consent to preserve life

question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Article 21

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law, and courts have read the right to health into it

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — Article 14: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law

B — Article 32: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. Answer C is the correct article for life and personal liberty

D — Article 19: Article 19 protects the six freedoms including speech and movement

⚠️ Exam Trap: Beware near-sounding options (Delhi vs New Delhi, Godavari vs Ganga).

💎 PNC Pearl: The right to emergency medical treatment has been recognised as part of Article 21

question: In which year did the Dandi March led by Mahatma Gandhi take place?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: d. 1930

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The Dandi March began on 12 March 1930 and launched the Civil Disobedience Movement by breaking the salt law

❌ Why Not Other Options?

A — 1942: 1942 was the year of the Quit India Movement

B — 1947: 1947 was the year of independence and partition

C — 1919: 1919 saw the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Rowlatt Act agitation

⚠️ Exam Trap: Beware near-sounding options (Delhi vs New Delhi, Godavari vs Ganga).

💎 PNC Pearl: Dates of national movements are frequently asked, so link each movement with its year and its immediate cause

question: Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana provides annual health cover per family of:
solution:

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The scheme provides a cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation to eligible beneficiary families

question: Which city is known as the "Pink City" of Rajasthan?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Jaipur

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Jaipur is called the Pink City because its old walled city was painted terracotta pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales

❌ Why Not Other Options?

question: Which is the longest river of India?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Ganga

🧠 Clinical Rationale: The Ganga is the longest river within India, flowing about 2,525 km from Gangotri to the Bay of Bengal

❌ Why Not Other Options?

💎 PNC Pearl: River basins determine water supply and vector breeding, so geography links directly with community health work

question: Under which Article can the President declare a National Emergency in India?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: b. Article 352

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim a National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion, after the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet

❌ Why Not Other Options?

⚠️ Exam Trap: Beware near-sounding options (Delhi vs New Delhi, Godavari vs Ganga).

question: Who was the first woman to become the President of India?
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: c. Pratibha Patil

🧠 Clinical Rationale: Pratibha Patil served as the President of India from 2007 to 2012 and was the first woman to hold the office

question: The World Health Organization is headquartered at:
solution:
✅ Correct Answer: a. Geneva

🧠 Clinical Rationale: WHO has its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, and works through six regional offices, with the South-East Asia Regional Office at New Delhi

❌ Why Not Other Options?

B — Vienna: Vienna hosts the IAEA and several UN agencies

⚠️ Exam Trap: Beware near-sounding options (Delhi vs New Delhi, Godavari vs Ganga).
